newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FEATURE - China or the peg? H.Kong ponders inflation.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - China or the peg? H.Kong ponders inflation.

text.p: Inflation is no stranger to Hong Kong, the rocky island outcrop that defied all odds to transform itself into a commercial metropolis.
In the space of 150 years, Hong Kong's relentless pursuit of prosperity generated double-digit growth rates almost always accompanied by high inflation.

Over the last 15 years, the British colony's growth rates have slowed, reflecting a shift in its economy from a manufacturing and exporting hub into a service-based economy geared to China's emergence.
But inflation has persisted.
While Hong Kong's lower growth rates reflect its transformation into a developed economy, inflation remains in line with the rest of this high-growth and still-developing region.
Traditionally, the Hong Kong dollar peg took the blame for inflation rates twice and sometimes three times higher than those of the United States.
Hong Kong's dollar link to the U.S., established in 1983 at a rate of HK$7.80, forces the British colony to follow U.S. monetary policy regardless of domestic economic conditions.

"Once you peg your currency, you don't have much discretion as far as interest rates go. You follow what happens in the United States with a risk premium for the country," said Paul Alapat, economist at Lehman Brothers.
If rates in the United States fell, Hong Kong was required to follow suit even if local circumstances warranted an interest rate increase.
CRITICISM IS TABOO
"On the domestic front, the most powerful argument against the Hong Kong dollar-U.S.dollar link is inflation," said Friedrich Wu, chief economist with DBS Securities.
Any criticism of the Hong Kong dollar peg is taboo in a colony that has relied heavily on the currency's stability through some turbulent times.
"This is a very controversial subject," said one economist.

The Hong Kong government resolutely refuses to accept that the U.S. dollar peg is entirely responsible for inflation in Hong Kong, pointing instead to China's rising demand on Hong Kong services as the main culprit.
"Insofar as tradeable goods are concerned, our inflation rate is more or less the same as that in the United States," Joseph Yam, chief executive of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, said recently.

"Because of the opening up of China, because of reform and the liberalisation of China, there has been huge demand on our services and as a result, prices of our services have increased faster than tradeable goods," Yam said.
Economists generally agree that the problem is restricted to the domestic economy, but they are less convinced that the China connection is as clear-cut and obvious as Yam suggested.

Most economists said that while China was certainly responsible for an overall expansion of Hong Kong's services sector, by far the strongest inflationary pressures were being felt in wage rates, which are soaring as employers struggle to find qualified, competent and skilled workers in a newly inadequate labour force.
WAGES UP, UNEMPLOYMENT UP

Ironically, the pressure on wage rates exists alongside an unemployment rate of about three percent. Once famed for full employment, Hong Kong now lacks low-skilled, manufacturing jobs, most of which have been transplanted into regions offering lower labour costs across the border in southern China.

"While it is difficult to pinpoint any single responsible factor for the stubbornly high inflation in Hong Kong, there is strong evidence so show that the uptrend in wages is, very possibly, the main culprit," said Wu.
Government data makes it almost impossible to confirm this theory, largely because monthly consumer price index data in Hong Kong do not include another key inflation suspect -- property prices.

The investment vehicle of choice for many Hong Kong residents, property prices reflect demand for one of the colony's scarcest commodities, signalling economic confidence and often the direction of the Hong Kong stock market.
In addition, Hong Kong pays most attention to seemingly the least relevant of three individual consumer price indices.
The government does provide a composite figure, but CPI(A), or data from the lowest income bracket in Hong Kong, is considered the headline figure.
"I agree the composite number is more reflective, but as a tradition no one is willing to use it," said Charles Li, chief economist at Natwest Markets. "Very strange, isn't it?"
The government's failure to include property in CPI suggests nobody really knows what Hong Kong's inflation rate is.
The gross domestic product deflator is considered a more accurate gauge, but it is released quarterly, with a time lag of at least six months, and is subject to constant revision.

The deflator does, however, show little discrepancy with CPI data, which have prompted a government inflation forecast of 6.8 percent for the year while most economists expect to see an economic growth rate of about 4.5 percent.
